spec.concept: The total stopping distance increases quadratically with speed because the braking distance depends on the square of the velocity.
spec.definition: Stopping distance is the total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver perceives a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to a full stop.

prediction.prompt: A car at 40 km/h needs about 21 m to stop (1 s to react, then braking). How many meters does it need at 80 km/h?

extremes.watch: Poor road conditions (low friction) drastically increase the quadratic term.
High performance braking still cannot overcome the speed squared rule.

misconceptions.label: Twice as fast, twice as far
misconceptions.why_tempting: Doubling speed doubling distance feels fair.
misconceptions.refutation: Braking distance grows with speed squared, so it is 4x; only the reaction part doubles: 22 + 41 = 63 m.
misconceptions.source_note: Page states the correct model; that this mistake is common is unverified

misconceptions.label: Everything quadruples
misconceptions.why_tempting: Once you know braking scales with speed squared, you apply it to all of it.
misconceptions.refutation: The 1 s reaction distance only doubles; only the braking part quadruples.
misconceptions.source_note: Page states the correct model; that this mistake is common is unverified
